title: Colicky abdominal pain and vomiting in a 45-year-old hairdresser
desc: This station involves a focused history and examination of a 45-year-old woman in a rural ED with 3 days of colicky periumbilical pain, bilious vomiting, no stool or flatus, and previous caesarean sections and appendicectomy. The candidate then interprets her observations, bloods, venous gas and abdominal X-ray report, names the diagnosis and differentials, and outlines resuscitation, surgical discussion, transfer and safety netting.
focus: Acute colicky abdominal pain with vomiting and obstipation: recognising and managing adhesive small bowel obstruction in a rural ED
stem: You are an intern working in a rural Emergency Department. Jaden, a 45-year-old hairdresser, has come in by ambulance with abdominal pain. The hospital has plain X-ray but no CT scanner and no on-site surgical service. The nearest general surgical service is at the regional base hospital. A nurse is with you and will carry out any instructions you give.
tasks: Take a focused history from the patient and perform a focused examination, telling the examiner what you are examining (10 minutes).

The examiner will give you her observations, blood results and venous gas, and an abdominal X-ray report. Interpret them, give your diagnosis and differentials, then outline your management approach and safety netting (5 minutes).
patient:
Role: You are Jaden, a 45-year-old hairdresser. You are lying on the trolley with a vomit bowl beside you. Every 5 to 10 minutes a wave of cramping pain comes and lasts a minute or two: you curl up and stop talking for a moment, then settle between waves. The examiner gives examination findings from the Exam findings below when the candidate says what they would examine.

Opening line: "I've got this awful cramping pain in my tummy and I keep being sick."

History (give only when asked)

The pain

  • In the middle of your tummy, around the belly button. It does not go anywhere else.
  • It came on suddenly 3 days ago.
  • Cramping. Waves of cramp every 5 to 10 minutes, each lasting a minute or two, coming more often since yesterday.
  • 8 out of 10 at its worst.
  • Paracetamol helped a little at first but not now. You tried a laxative and it did not help.
  • You couldn't concentrate and have taken days off work.

Vomiting and eating

  • Nausea and vomiting for 3 days, about 5 times. Large amounts each time.
  • At first it was food, now it is green-yellow (bile). No blood.
  • You can't eat anything.

Bowels (give these only to specific questions; if asked a vague "anything else?", say "Like what?")

  • No bowel motion for 3 days. The last one was 4 days ago, small and hard, with no blood or mucus. Before this your bowels were regular.
  • You have not passed wind for 3 days.
  • Your belly looks a bit bigger than normal, but not hugely swollen.
  • No diarrhoea, no blood from the back passage.

Other questions

  • If asked about sick contacts or what might have caused it: "My son had gastro a week ago, but he's well recovered from it. I don't think anyone else in my family has got it from him."
  • No recent travel.
  • No sore joints, red eyes, skin rashes or mouth ulcers. No weight loss.
  • If asked about periods or pregnancy: periods are light and irregular on the mini pill; you don't think you could be pregnant.
  • No fever, chest pain or urinary symptoms.

Past history

  • Depression for 10 years, well controlled.
  • Two caesarean sections, 10 and 13 years ago.
  • Appendix removed at 21.

Medications

  • Progestogen-only pill (mini pill) daily.
  • Venlafaxine 75 mg daily.
  • A multivitamin.

Allergies

  • If asked "any allergies?": tree nuts. "My whole face and throat get swollen."
  • Only if asked directly about medicine allergies or penicillin: penicillin. "I get a bad skin rash, swollen tongue and lip."

Family history

  • No inflammatory bowel disease, coeliac disease or bowel cancer in the family.
  • Father: high blood pressure and type 1 diabetes. Mother: breast cancer at 60, now well. Brother well. Your children, 13 and 10, are well.

Social history

  • Hairdresser. Live with your husband and 2 children.
  • Non-smoker. One glass of wine with dinner. No drugs.
  • Fully independent.

Ideas, concerns, expectations: you wondered if you caught your son's gastro, but this feels different. If asked what worries you: "My friend was diagnosed with bowel cancer at my age, I hope it's nothing like that." You want something for the pain and to know what is going on.

The nurse and how Jaden changes

  • If the candidate asks for observations, the nurse gives the ones under Exam findings.
  • Partway through, the nurse says: "She's just vomited again, about 400 mL of green fluid."
  • If the candidate orders IV analgesia, a few minutes later Jaden's pain eases to about 4 out of 10 and she answers more easily. If not, she stays at 8 out of 10 during waves.
  • If the candidate orders an antiemetic, IV fluids or a nasogastric tube, the nurse says she will arrange it.
  • If the candidate orders metoclopramide, the nurse says she will arrange it (do not prompt); the examiner notes this for the antiemetic item in Part 2.
  • If the candidate asks for bloods, a gas or imaging in Part 1, the examiner says the results will be given in Part 2.

Exam findings (examiner gives each only when the candidate says what they examine)

  • Observations: HR 108 regular, BP 118/76, RR 18, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 37.4 °C, BGL 5.8 mmol/L.
  • General: uncomfortable, curls up with waves of pain and settles between them. Bilious vomit in the bowl. Alert.
  • Hydration: dry mucous membranes, CRT 2 seconds, warm peripheries.
  • Hands, face and neck: no anaemia, jaundice or lymphadenopathy, including the supraclavicular fossae.
  • Abdomen, inspection: mildly distended. Well-healed Pfannenstiel scar and a right iliac fossa (gridiron) scar. No visible peristalsis.
  • Hernial orifices and scars: no inguinal, femoral, umbilical or incisional hernia. Cough impulse negative.
  • Palpation: mild diffuse tenderness, most around the umbilicus. No guarding, rigidity or rebound. No masses. No organomegaly.
  • Percussion: tympanic centrally. No shifting dullness.
  • Auscultation: high-pitched, tinkling bowel sounds.
  • PR (if requested): empty rectum, no blood, no mass.
  • Heart and lungs: normal.
  • Everything else normal.

check.x: Professionalism
Washes hands, introduces self, confirms the patient's identity, acknowledges her pain and offers analgesia and an antiemetic early, without waiting until the end of the history.
Uses plain language and empathy, pauses during waves of pain, explains each part of the examination before doing it, and keeps the history focused.
History
Characterises the pain:
check.d: Critical: at least site, onset/character and timing (3 of 5).

kids.x: Site and radiation: central, periumbilical, no radiation
Onset and character: sudden onset 3 days ago, cramping and colicky
Timing: comes and goes in waves every few minutes, more frequent since yesterday
Severity and modifying factors: 8/10, paracetamol helped a little at first, a laxative did not help
Impact: could not concentrate, has taken days off work

check.x: Characterises the vomiting: for 3 days, about 5 times, large volume, food then bile, no blood, and she cannot eat.

Asks specifically about bowel motions and flatus and elicits obstipation: no bowel motion for 3 days (last 4 days ago, small and hard, no blood or mucus), no flatus for 3 days, belly a bit larger than normal.
Asks questions to rule out the differentials:

kids.x: Large bowel obstruction: marked distension, late small-volume vomiting (she has neither)
Inflammatory bowel disease: bloody diarrhoea and extra-intestinal features (joints, eyes, skin, mouth ulcers)
Gastroenteritis: diarrhoea, travel and sick contacts, eliciting the son's gastro a week ago
Appendicitis: establishes the appendix has been removed

check.x: Asks about previous abdominal surgery and elicits two caesarean sections (10 and 13 years ago) and an appendicectomy at 21.
Takes a past medical history: depression for 10 years, well controlled.
Takes a medication history: progestogen-only pill daily, venlafaxine 75 mg daily, multivitamin.
Asks directly about drug and other allergies and clarifies each reaction: penicillin (rash with tongue and lip swelling) and tree nuts (face and throat swelling).
check.d: Penicillin is only given if the candidate asks about medicine allergies directly. Teaching point: always ask specifically about medicine allergies.

check.x: Asks about the possibility of pregnancy (periods, contraception) before imaging and drug treatment.
Takes a family history: no IBD, coeliac disease or bowel cancer; father with hypertension and type 1 diabetes; mother with breast cancer at 60, now well.
Takes a social history: hairdresser, lives with husband and 2 children, non-smoker, one glass of wine with dinner, no drugs, independent.
Explores her ideas, concerns and expectations and elicits her fear of bowel cancer because a friend was diagnosed at her age.
Examination
Asks for the vital signs and assesses hydration: HR 108, dry mucous membranes, CRT and peripheral perfusion.
Inspects the abdomen: mild distension, Pfannenstiel and right iliac fossa scars.
Examines the hernial orifices and scars (inguinal, femoral, umbilical, incisional) with a cough impulse.
Palpates gently for tenderness, guarding, rigidity, rebound and masses, looking for peritonism.
Percusses and auscultates the abdomen: tympanic, high-pitched tinkling bowel sounds.
Asks for a PR examination (empty rectum, no blood or mass).
Interpretation

Interprets the observations: HR rising from 108 (white) to 122 (yellow zone, calls for a clinical review), SBP falling from 118 to 106, ongoing vomiting and no urine output, meaning significant fluid loss.
Identifies a prerenal AKI (creatinine 102 against a baseline of 64, KDIGO stage 1; urea 11.2) and hypokalaemia (K 3.3) from vomiting and third-space losses.
Notes haemoconcentration (Hb 146, baseline 128), the non-specific WCC 11.8 and CRP 18, and the negative beta-hCG.
Interprets the venous gas as a hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis from vomiting, and states that a normal lactate does not exclude bowel ischaemia.

Interprets the X-ray: dilated central small bowel up to 4 cm (above 3 cm) with valvulae conniventes and multiple air-fluid levels, a collapsed colon with no colonic or caecal dilatation, and no free gas, so small bowel obstruction. States that a plain film cannot show the transition point or ischaemia and CT is needed.

Gives the diagnosis as small bowel obstruction, most likely from adhesions after her caesarean sections and appendicectomy, justified by at least 3 of: sudden colicky periumbilical pain, early large bilious vomiting, no stool or flatus for 3 days, mild distension, tinkling bowel sounds, previous surgery, the X-ray.

Includes large bowel obstruction as a differential and explains why it is less likely (mild distension, early large-volume vomiting, collapsed colon on X-ray), plus at least one other with a feature for or against it (strangulation or closed loop, incarcerated hernia, gastroenteritis, malignancy).
Management

Nil by mouth, IV access, an IV isotonic crystalloid bolus (e.g. 500 mL 0.9% sodium chloride) with reassessment, then replacement fluid covering ongoing and NG losses, with potassium once urine output is confirmed; IDC and fluid balance chart (target at least 0.5 mL/kg/h).
check.d: Critical elements: nil by mouth, IV isotonic crystalloid bolus with reassessment, and urine output monitoring (IDC/fluid balance). Ongoing replacement, potassium timing and the numeric target are desirable.

check.x: Inserts a nasogastric tube on free drainage with regular aspiration.

Gives titrated IV opioid analgesia (e.g. morphine; avoids tramadol and pethidine with venlafaxine) and a non-prokinetic antiemetic (e.g. ondansetron, watching for serotonin toxicity with venlafaxine), avoiding metoclopramide in mechanical obstruction.

Discusses early with the general surgeon at the regional base hospital and arranges transfer for admission and CT abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast (to find the transition point, a closed loop or ischaemia).
States the indications for urgent surgery: peritonitis, strangulation or ischaemia, closed loop, or failure to settle with non-operative management.

Documents the allergies prominently (penicillin with lip and tongue swelling, tree nuts) and notes that antibiotics are not routine and, if needed, must avoid penicillins; flags that oral venlafaxine won't be absorbed with NBM/NG on free drainage, hands this to the receiving team, and watches for discontinuation symptoms.
Safety netting

Answers Jaden's question about bowel cancer honestly in plain words: the most likely cause is scar tissue from her operations, cancer is less likely (no blood, no family history, no weight loss) and the CT will look for the cause; and tells her to tell staff at once if the pain becomes constant or worse, or she feels hot or faint.
check.d: If Jaden adds 'Will I need an operation?', credit an honest plain answer (it often settles without an operation, but she may need one) within this item.

check.x: Sets escalation triggers before and during transfer (senior review for any yellow zone value, rapid response for red): at least 4 of a rising heart rate, falling BP, fever, pain that becomes constant or out of proportion, new guarding or rigidity, a rising lactate, falling urine output.

part2.lead: Here are Jaden's observations, her blood results and venous gas, and the abdominal X-ray report.
part2.patient:
After the candidate answers the cancer question, Jaden may add: "Will I need an operation?" (credit within item 40).

She is relieved if told cancer is unlikely and that this often settles without an operation, but anxious about the transfer and the tube in her nose. If the candidate uses jargon such as "adhesions" or "NG tube", ask: "What does that mean?"

handover.label: Observations
handover.result: On room air. No urine passed since arrival at 14:10.
handover.model:
• Examiner note: the 15:10 pain score is blank on the chart. If IV analgesia was ordered in Part 1, tell the candidate the pain score is 4 and analgesia has been given; otherwise it is 8 and no analgesia has been given.
  • Read: at 14:10 HR 108, BP 118/76, RR 18, SpO2 97% on room air and temperature 37.4 °C are all in the white zone. At 15:10 HR has risen to 122, in the yellow zone; SBP has fallen to 106 (white), temperature 37.6 °C. She has vomited again and passed no urine.
  • Meaning: a rising tachycardia, falling BP, ongoing vomiting and no urine output point to significant fluid loss from vomiting and third-spacing into the bowel. Afebrile, which is reassuring, but a rising HR is also an early sign of strangulation.
  • Changes: the yellow zone HR calls for a clinical review now (the candidate, escalating to the senior medical officer per local escalation rules). Fluid resuscitation, analgesia, hourly observations and fluid balance; a rapid response if any value enters the red zone.

rows.note: Arrived by ambulance. Triage ATS 2: severe abdominal pain, vomiting
Vomited about 400 mL green fluid; no urine passed. Pain score: see examiner. Doctor informed

handover.label: Bloods and venous blood gas
handover.result: Collected 14:30 at cannulation. Haemolysis index normal. Baseline values from bloods at this hospital in 2025.
handover.model:
• Read: creatinine 102 against a baseline of 64 with urea 11.2: AKI (KDIGO stage 1), urea raised out of proportion, a prerenal pattern. Na 134, K 3.3 and Cl 94 are low. Hb 146 against a baseline of 128 shows haemoconcentration. Venous pH 7.46, HCO3 31, BE +6 with an appropriate pCO2: metabolic alkalosis. Lactate 1.3 normal. WCC 11.8 with neutrophilia and CRP 18 mildly raised. Lipase, LFTs, INR normal. Beta-hCG negative.
  • Meaning: dehydration from vomiting and third-space losses causing a prerenal AKI and a hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis. The inflammatory rise is non-specific; a normal lactate does not exclude ischaemia because it rises late. Pancreatitis and biliary causes are unlikely, and she is not pregnant, so CT can proceed.
  • Changes: IV 0.9% sodium chloride (its chloride corrects the alkalosis) with potassium as a premixed bag once she is passing urine, IDC and fluid balance, repeat UEC; group and hold done for the receiving hospital.

rows.n: not valid in acute kidney injury

handover.label: Abdominal X-ray and erect chest X-ray
handover.result:
Examination: abdominal X-ray, supine and erect AP views, with an erect PA chest X-ray. 14:50.

Clinical details: 45-year-old woman. 3 days of colicky periumbilical pain, large-volume bilious vomiting, no stool or flatus for 3 days, mild distension, tinkling bowel sounds. Previous caesarean sections and appendicectomy. ?Bowel obstruction.

Findings:

  • Small bowel: multiple dilated, centrally placed loops of small bowel up to 4.0 cm in diameter, with valvulae conniventes crossing the full width of the bowel. On the erect view, multiple air-fluid levels at differing heights.
  • Large bowel: little gas in the colon and rectum. No colonic dilatation; the caecum is not dilated.
  • Free gas: no free gas under the diaphragm on the erect chest X-ray.
  • Other abdominal features: no pneumatosis, portal venous gas or pneumobilia. No radio-opaque calculi. No abnormal soft tissue mass seen.
  • Chest: lungs clear, normal heart size, no effusion.
  • Bones: no acute bony abnormality.

Conclusion: dilated small bowel with air-fluid levels and a collapsed colon, in keeping with small bowel obstruction. No pneumoperitoneum. Plain films cannot assess the cause, transition point or bowel viability; CT abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast is recommended.
handover.model:
• Read: central dilated loops up to 4 cm (above the 3 cm limit for small bowel; 3-6-9 rule) with valvulae conniventes, stepladder air-fluid levels on the erect film, and little gas in a non-dilated colon and caecum (below 6 and 9 cm). No free gas, pneumatosis or portal venous gas.
  • Meaning: small bowel obstruction, proximal dilatation with distal collapse. With two caesarean sections and an appendicectomy and no hernia, adhesions are the most likely cause. A collapsed colon argues against large bowel obstruction; no free gas means no perforation is seen.
  • Changes: confirms the need for NG decompression, IV fluids and surgical referral. CT with IV contrast (gold standard) is needed for the transition point, a closed loop and ischaemia, so it is arranged at the receiving hospital as agreed with the surgeon.

ask: You are now calling the general surgical registrar at the regional base hospital. Please give an ISBAR handover of Jaden, including your interpretation of these results.
What is your most likely diagnosis, and what else would you consider? Justify your answer.
Outline your management of Jaden now, here in the rural emergency department, and the triggers for escalation before transfer.
Jaden asks you, "Could this be bowel cancer, like my friend?" Please answer her.
expect:
• Identify: self, intern at the rural ED; Jaden, 45.
  • Situation: small bowel obstruction, most likely adhesional, with dehydration and AKI; HR rising; requesting transfer under general surgery.
  • Background: 3 days of colicky periumbilical pain, large bilious vomits, no stool or flatus for 3 days, mild distension, tinkling bowel sounds, no hernia, no peritonism; two caesarean sections and appendicectomy; venlafaxine, mini pill; penicillin allergy with lip and tongue swelling.
  • Assessment: HR 108 to 122 (yellow), SBP 118 to 106, no urine; prerenal AKI (creatinine 102, baseline 64), K 3.3, metabolic alkalosis; lactate 1.3 normal but does not exclude ischaemia; WCC 11.8, CRP 18 non-specific; hCG negative; X-ray SBO, collapsed colon, no free gas.
  • Recommendation: accept for transfer and CT; NBM, NG tube, IV fluids started; any advice before transfer.

Adhesive small bowel obstruction: sudden colicky periumbilical pain, early large bilious vomiting, no stool or flatus for 3 days, mild distension, tinkling bowel sounds, previous caesareans and appendicectomy, X-ray dilated small bowel with collapsed colon.

  • Large bowel obstruction (less likely): for: colic, obstipation; against: mild distension, early large vomits, collapsed colon.
  • Strangulated or closed-loop SBO (must not miss): for: rising HR, WCC 11.8; against: colicky pain, no peritonism, afebrile, normal lactate.
  • Incarcerated hernia: against: hernial orifices and scars normal.
  • Gastroenteritis: for: son's gastro; against: no diarrhoea, no flatus.
  • Malignancy: her concern; against: no blood, no family history, no weight loss.

1. Nil by mouth, IV access, bloods sent (group and hold).
  2. IV 0.9% sodium chloride bolus (e.g. 500 mL), reassess, then replacement for ongoing and NG losses; potassium as a premixed bag (no faster than 10 mmol/h peripherally) once passing urine.
  3. IDC and fluid balance (at least 0.5 mL/kg/h, about 34 mL/h).
  4. NG tube on free drainage with regular aspiration.
  5. Titrated IV opioid (e.g. morphine; avoid tramadol and pethidine with venlafaxine); ondansetron (watch for serotonin toxicity with venlafaxine), not metoclopramide.
  6. Early call to the general surgeon and transfer for admission and CT with IV contrast.
  7. Urgent surgery for peritonitis, strangulation or ischaemia, closed loop, or failure to settle.
  8. Allergies documented (no penicillins); flags that oral venlafaxine won't be absorbed with NBM/NG on free drainage, hands this to the receiving team, and watches for discontinuation symptoms.
  9. Escalation triggers before transfer (senior review for a yellow zone value, rapid response for red): rising HR, falling BP, fever, constant pain, guarding or rigidity, rising lactate, falling urine output.

• Cancer question: honest and plain: most likely a blockage from scar tissue (adhesions) from her operations; cancer is less likely (no blood, no family history, no weight loss) and the scan will look for the cause.
  • Tell staff at once: pain becoming constant or worse, feeling hot or faint.

ddx.for: Sudden colicky periumbilical pain, early large bilious vomiting, no stool or flatus for 3 days, mild distension and tinkling bowel sounds after two caesarean sections and an appendicectomy, with dilated small bowel and a collapsed colon on X-ray.
She has colicky pain and has not passed stool or flatus for 3 days, with a small hard stool before that.
ddx.against: Distension is mild, the vomiting was early, large and bilious, and the colon is collapsed on X-ray.

ddx.dx: Strangulated or closed-loop small bowel obstruction with ischaemia
ddx.for: Her heart rate is rising to 122 and she has a mildly raised WCC after 3 days of severe pain.
ddx.against: The pain is still colicky, she is afebrile with no guarding or rebound, and the lactate is normal.

ddx.for: She has two caesarean scars and a gridiron scar, and femoral hernias are easily missed in women.
ddx.against: The hernial orifices and scars are normal with no cough impulse.

ddx.for: Her son had gastro a week ago.
ddx.against: She has no diarrhoea, has passed no stool or flatus for 3 days, nobody else is unwell, and the X-ray shows obstruction.

ddx.for: She is 45 and worried because a friend was diagnosed with bowel cancer at her age.
ddx.against: She has no family history of bowel cancer, no blood or mucus in her stool, no weight loss and no mass on examination.

guide:
In Part 1, Jaden answers the history. The examiner gives findings from the Exam findings only when the candidate says what they would examine. Jaden gives the bowel and flatus history only to specific questions, and gives the penicillin allergy only if asked directly about medicine allergies. Partway through, the nurse reports another large bilious vomit. If the candidate asks for investigations in Part 1, say they will be given in Part 2. In Part 2, hand over the observations, the bloods and gas, and the X-ray report, then ask all four questions in order. The 15:10 pain score is blank: give 4 if IV analgesia was ordered in Part 1, otherwise 8. After the candidate answers the cancer question, Jaden may add whether she will need an operation.

A high-performing candidate characterises the pain fully, asks specifically about bowel motions, flatus and previous surgery, rules out large bowel obstruction, IBD, gastroenteritis and appendicitis, clarifies both allergies and offers analgesia early. They examine hydration, scars, all hernial orifices and the abdomen for peritonism. In Part 2 they recognise the yellow zone heart rate, a prerenal AKI and a hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis, state that a normal lactate does not exclude ischaemia, read the X-ray as small bowel obstruction and say CT is needed. They resuscitate, decompress with an NG tube, avoid metoclopramide, call the surgeon early and transfer, and answer the cancer question honestly.

A borderline candidate takes the pain history but does not ask about flatus or previous surgery, misses the penicillin allergy, or omits the hernial orifices. They may call the gas normal or be reassured by the lactate, plan oral fluids or metoclopramide, or keep her in the rural hospital waiting for her to settle, without early surgical discussion and transfer.
explain:
Diagnosis: adhesive small bowel obstruction

Jaden has the cardinal features of bowel obstruction: colicky abdominal pain, vomiting, distension and absolute constipation (no stool and no flatus). Sudden, central, colicky pain with early, large-volume bilious vomiting and only mild distension points to the small bowel. Her two caesarean sections and appendicectomy are the risk factor. Adhesions from previous abdominal or pelvic surgery are the most common cause of small bowel obstruction in adults.

Small versus large bowel obstruction

  • Small bowel: central colic, early and large vomiting (bilious in proximal obstruction, faeculent later in distal), mild to moderate distension, constipation later.
  • Large bowel: constipation and marked distension early, vomiting late and small in volume, often from a colorectal cancer or volvulus.

Jaden's early large vomits and mild distension, and her collapsed colon on X-ray, place this in the small bowel.

Risk factors and causes of SBO

Previous abdominal surgery (adhesions, the commonest cause), hernia (especially irreducible), malrotation, Crohn's strictures, appendicitis and other inflammatory masses, and gallstone ileus. In the history, rule out the differentials directly: large bowel obstruction (late small vomits, marked distension), IBD (bloody diarrhoea, extra-intestinal features), gastroenteritis (diarrhoea, travel, contacts) and appendicitis (here already removed). On examination, look at every hernial orifice and scar, and for peritonism.

Interpreting the results

  • Observations: a heart rate rising into the yellow zone with a falling BP and no urine output means significant fluid loss and calls for a clinical review. A rising HR is also an early sign of strangulation.
  • Bloods and gas: vomiting and third-space losses give a prerenal AKI and haemoconcentration. Loss of gastric acid and chloride, with aldosterone driving potassium loss, gives a hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis. Lactate rises late in ischaemia, so a normal value does not exclude it. A negative beta-hCG matters before imaging in a woman of reproductive age.
  • Abdominal X-ray: dilated loops with air-fluid levels, proximal dilatation with distal collapse. The 3-6-9 rule: small bowel above 3 cm, colon above 6 cm and caecum above 9 cm are dilated. Small bowel is central with valvulae conniventes crossing the full width; colon is peripheral with haustra.
  • CT abdomen with IV contrast: the gold standard. It shows the transition point and cause, a closed loop, and signs of ischaemia.

Management

Look for features of strangulation: peritonitis, fever, leucocytosis, tachycardia, acidosis or pain that becomes continuous. Then:

  • Nil by mouth, IV fluid resuscitation (0.9% sodium chloride corrects the chloride-responsive alkalosis), then replacement for ongoing and NG losses.
  • Correct electrolytes: potassium as a premixed bag, no faster than 10 mmol/h peripherally, once urine output is confirmed.
  • Nasogastric decompression on free drainage with regular aspiration.
  • Titrated IV opioid analgesia (e.g. morphine). Because she takes venlafaxine (an SNRI), avoid serotonergic opioids such as tramadol and pethidine, and use fentanyl with caution.
  • An antiemetic that is not prokinetic, such as ondansetron, watching for serotonin toxicity (and QT prolongation) alongside venlafaxine; metoclopramide is avoided in mechanical obstruction.
  • IDC and fluid balance chart.
  • Early surgical consultation. Urgent surgery if ischaemia or strangulation is suspected, for peritonitis or a closed loop, or if the obstruction fails to settle.

The WSES (Bologna) guidelines support non-operative management of adhesive SBO without signs of strangulation, including water-soluble contrast, which is both diagnostic and therapeutic; that decision belongs to the receiving surgical team.

In a rural ED without CT or a surgeon: discuss early with the general surgeon at the referral centre and arrange transfer for CT and admission, with resuscitation, NG decompression and clear escalation triggers during the wait and the transfer.

Patient factors

Her penicillin reaction (rash with lip and tongue swelling) is a severe immediate allergy and must be documented; antibiotics are not routine in uncomplicated SBO and, if needed, follow eTG for penicillin allergy. With an NG tube on free drainage, oral venlafaxine will not be absorbed; flag it to the receiving team and watch for discontinuation symptoms. Vomiting makes the progestogen-only pill unreliable, which she should be told before discharge.

Safety netting

Staff escalate for a rising heart rate, falling BP, fever, constant or worsening pain, new guarding, a rising lactate or falling urine output, any of which may mean strangulation. Jaden's fear of bowel cancer deserves an honest, plain answer: the likely cause is scar tissue, and the CT will look for anything else. Adhesive obstruction can recur; after discharge she returns to ED for crampy pain, vomiting, bloating or not passing wind.
points: Colicky pain, vomiting, distension and absolute constipation are the cardinal features of bowel obstruction. Always ask specifically about flatus and previous abdominal surgery.
Adhesions from previous abdominal or pelvic surgery, including caesarean section and appendicectomy, are the most common cause of small bowel obstruction in adults.
Early large-volume vomiting with mild distension points to small bowel obstruction; marked early distension with late small vomits points to large bowel obstruction.
On plain X-ray use the 3-6-9 rule (small bowel above 3 cm, colon above 6 cm, caecum above 9 cm). CT with IV contrast is the gold standard for the transition point, a closed loop and ischaemia.
Vomiting and third-space losses cause a prerenal AKI and a hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis. A normal lactate does not exclude ischaemia.
Manage with nil by mouth, IV fluids with potassium, NG decompression, analgesia and a non-prokinetic antiemetic. In a rural ED, call the surgeon early and transfer.
refs: Ten Broek RPG, Krielen P, Di Saverio S, et al. Bologna guidelines for diagnosis and management of adhesive small bowel obstruction (ASBO): 2017 update of the evidence-based guidelines from the World Society of Emergency Surgery ASBO working group. World J Emerg Surg 2018;13:24.
Therapeutic Guidelines. Pain and Analgesia: acute pain management. Melbourne: Therapeutic Guidelines Limited; current version.
